principles.title: Tend only what is yours to tend
principles.motto: Your judgments are your garden; the weather belongs to the sky.
principles.essence: Some things are in your hands: your judgments, your choices, your effort, the way you meet what comes. Most things are not: other people, the past, your reputation, the weather, the final outcome. Pour your strength into the first circle and loosen your grip on the second, and you stop losing battles that were never yours to fight.
principles.depth: Epictetus opens his Handbook (the Enchiridion, written down by his student Arrian in the early second century) with a single division: some things are up to us, and some are not. Up to us are opinion, desire, aversion and our own actions. Not up to us are body, property, reputation and office. Suffering, he says, comes from treating the second list as if it were the first. Modern psychology found the same seam. Julian Rotter's work on locus of control (1966) showed that people who see their own actions as mattering tend to act more and cope better. Martin Seligman and Steven Maier (1967) showed the dark side: animals taught that nothing they did mattered stopped trying even when escape became possible, a pattern they called learned helplessness. Aaron Beck and Albert Ellis, founders of cognitive therapy, both credited Epictetus's line that people are disturbed not by things but by their judgments about things. Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman's research on stress (1984) adds a practical rule: change what can be changed (problem-focused coping) and work on your response to what cannot (emotion-focused coping). The real skill is sorting well, again and again, many times a day.

tales.title: The Leg That Did Not Break Him
tales.who: Epictetus, a slave who became a Stoic teacher; his master Epaphroditus
tales.where: Rome, then Nicopolis in western Greece
tales.source: Arrian's Discourses and Handbook of Epictetus; the leg story from Celsus, as quoted by Origen in Against Celsus 7.53; Simplicius on his lameness
tales.tale:
A young man limps across a marble floor in Rome, carrying a tray. His name is Epictetus, which in Greek means simply "acquired", a thing that was bought. He was born around 50 AD in Hierapolis, a town in what is now Turkey, and he belongs to Epaphroditus, a freed slave who rose to serve the emperor Nero. The young man owns nothing. Not his bed, not his days, not even his name.

There is a story about his leg. As it is told by Celsus, a Greek writer whose words survive because the Christian scholar Origen quoted them, the master once twisted his slave's leg in some cruel game. Epictetus watched and said quietly, "You will break it." The master twisted harder. The leg broke. And Epictetus said, in the same calm voice, "Did I not tell you that you would break it?" Other ancient writers say he was simply lame from childhood, or from an illness. No one can be sure. But the story lived because it fit the man.

Somehow, in that house, he was allowed to study with Musonius Rufus, a Stoic teacher. Somehow, later, he was set free. He taught philosophy in Rome until around 93 AD, when the emperor Domitian drove the philosophers out of the city. Epictetus went to Nicopolis, a port on the west coast of Greece, and opened a small school. Young men came from across the empire to hear the old lame teacher who had once been property.

What did he teach them? Mostly one thing, turned in the light from every side. Some things are in our power, and some are not. Your body can be chained. Your money can be taken. Your leg can be broken. But your judgment, your choice of how to meet the chain, no one can reach. "I must die," he said to his students. "Must I die groaning too?"

He never wrote a book. His student Arrian wrote down his talks, the Discourses, and a short summary, the Handbook. For nearly two thousand years, soldiers and emperors, prisoners and students have carried those pages in their pockets and in their heads.

A man who did not own his own leg found the one thing that could never be owned by anyone else.
tales.reveals: Epictetus had almost nothing in his control, and so he saw clearly the one thing that always is: his own judgment and choice. His life shows that this freedom does not wait for good circumstances; it can be found even inside the worst ones.

tales.title: Entering the World of Epictetus
tales.who: James Bond Stockdale, United States Navy pilot and prisoner of war
tales.where: Hoa Lo prison, Hanoi, North Vietnam
tales.source: Stockdale's lecture and essay Courage Under Fire: Testing Epictetus's Doctrines in a Laboratory of Human Behavior (1993); In Love and War, with Sybil Stockdale (1984); his Medal of Honor citation
tales.tale:
On the ninth of September 1965, gunfire tore through the plane of Commander James Stockdale over North Vietnam. He pulled the ejection handle and drifted down on his parachute toward a small village, with perhaps thirty seconds of open sky left to him. In those seconds, he later wrote, he whispered to himself that he was leaving the world of technology and entering the world of Epictetus.

He had met the old slave almost by chance. A few years before, as a navy officer studying at Stanford University, he had been given a copy of the Handbook by a philosophy professor named Philip Rhinelander. Stockdale read it the way a pilot reads the manual of a new aircraft: closely, again and again, never knowing he would need it.

He landed among angry villagers and was beaten. One leg was badly broken and would never heal straight. Then came Hoa Lo, an old French prison in Hanoi that the American prisoners called the Hanoi Hilton. He would stay a prisoner for seven and a half years. As a senior officer, he was singled out. He spent four years in solitary confinement and two in leg irons, and he was tortured, by his own count, about fifteen times.

In the dark he sorted his life into two piles, as Epictetus taught. Not his: the walls, the guards, the ropes, the date of his release, even his body. His: his judgments, his loyalty, his word to the men around him. The prisoners talked through the walls with a tapping code, letters set in a square of five rows and five columns, and Stockdale's rules for resisting travelled from cell to cell, tap by tap.

In 1969 his captors planned to film him for propaganda. Alone in a room, he cut his own scalp with a razor and beat his face with a stool until no camera could use him. It was terrible, and it was his choice, the one thing in that room that was.

He came home on the twelfth of February 1973, limping, and lived until 2005. He never said the Stoic way was easy. He said it held.

Walls can take a man's sky. They cannot reach what he decides inside.
tales.reveals: Stockdale shows that the line between what is yours and what is not is not a comfortable idea but a working tool under pressure. By giving up hope of controlling his captors, he kept full command of his own conduct, and helped other men keep theirs.

practice: Each morning, draw two short columns for the day ahead: "mine" and "not mine". Put your effort into the first and say one sentence of release for the second.
When worry or anger rises (in traffic, at work, over the news), ask quietly: is this up to me? If yes, take one action. If no, breathe and let your opinion of it soften.
Turn one outcome goal into a process goal: not "get the job" but "send three careful applications and practise the interview twice".
Journal: what is one thing I keep trying to control that belongs to someone else? What would I gain, and what would they gain, if I let it go?
principles.shadow: Tending only your own garden can become an excuse for indifference, a shrug of "not my problem" at injustice or a neighbor's need. Your choices include how you speak up and how you help; the Stoics called themselves citizens of the world, not hermits.

principles.title: Trust your own mind
principles.motto: Listen to the quiet voice first, then test it in daylight.
principles.essence: You were given a mind of your own, able to see, weigh and judge. Do not hand it over to the loudest voice, the oldest custom or the crowd, even when standing alone is uncomfortable. Trust what you have honestly seen, and keep testing it.
principles.depth: Emerson put it plainly in his essay Self-Reliance (1841): "To believe your own thought, to believe that what is true for you in your private heart is true for all men, that is genius." Kant had said something close in What Is Enlightenment? (1784): dare to know, have the courage to use your own understanding without another's guidance. Psychology shows why this takes courage. In Solomon Asch's line experiments (1951), people asked to match the length of lines went along with a group's plainly wrong answer on roughly a third of the test trials, and about three quarters gave in at least once. Yet when even one other person gave the true answer, conformity dropped sharply: a single ally makes independence easier. Albert Bandura's idea of self-efficacy (1977) adds that belief in your own capacity grows through small experiences of mastery, not through slogans. John Stuart Mill, in On Liberty (1859), warned that a person who knows only his own side of a case knows little even of that. So self-trust is not stubbornness. It is the habit of looking for yourself, saying what you see, and staying open to better evidence. Trust your mind the way a sailor trusts a compass: checked often, and followed when it holds.

tales.title: The Sermon That Closed a Door
tales.who: Ralph Waldo Emerson; the graduating class of Harvard Divinity School; the scholar Andrews Norton
tales.where: Divinity Hall chapel, Harvard, Cambridge, Massachusetts
tales.source: Emerson's Divinity School Address (15 July 1838); his letter to Henry Ware Jr. (October 1838); Andrews Norton's newspaper attack (August 1838) and his Discourse on the Latest Form of Infidelity (1839)
tales.tale:
It is a Sunday evening in July, warm, the windows of the small chapel open to the summer air. On the fifteenth of July 1838, a tall thin man of thirty-five stands up in Divinity Hall at Harvard to speak to the graduating class of the divinity school, a handful of young men about to become ministers. Their professors sit and listen. His name is Ralph Waldo Emerson. He had once been a minister himself, until he left his Boston pulpit because he could no longer lead a ceremony he did not believe in.

He begins with the beauty of the season: the grass growing, the buds bursting, the air sweet with the breath of the pine. Then he turns, gently, and says what he has come to say. Men have come to speak of God, he tells them, as if God were dead. Faith is being handed down secondhand, like an old coat. "Let me admonish you, first of all, to go alone," he says, "to refuse the good models, even those which are sacred in the imagination of men, and dare to love God without mediator or veil."

The room is very quiet. Some of the students are thrilled. Their teachers are not.

Within weeks the storm came. Andrews Norton, a respected Harvard scholar, attacked the address in a Boston newspaper, and the next year he called this new thinking "the latest form of infidelity". Friends wrote anxious letters. Emerson's old colleague Henry Ware Jr. asked him to defend his arguments. Emerson answered kindly, but he would not fight. He wrote, in effect, that he did not know how to argue for what he had simply seen; he could only say it.

So he went home to Concord, to his garden and his study and his long walks, and kept writing. Harvard did not invite him back to speak for nearly thirty years. The door stayed shut while his books crossed oceans.

Then, in 1866, Harvard gave him an honorary degree, and in 1867 asked him back to give a great public address. The young men who had heard him in that chapel were grey now. Slowly, the world had walked toward the place where he had once stood alone.

He had not shouted. He had not begged. He had trusted what he saw, and let time do the arguing.
tales.reveals: Emerson's self-trust cost him the approval of the most powerful institution in his world, and he paid without bitterness. His story shows that trusting your own mind often means accepting a long season of being unwelcome, and that quiet steadiness persuades better than a fight.

tales.title: Bread for Letters
tales.who: Frederick Douglass (then Frederick Bailey), an enslaved boy; Sophia and Hugh Auld
tales.where: Fells Point, Baltimore, Maryland
tales.source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845), chapters 6 and 7
tales.tale:
A small boy sits beside a kind woman in a house in Baltimore, and she points to a letter. A. Then B. Then C. The boy is about eight years old. He has been sent from a plantation on Maryland's Eastern Shore to serve in the city home of Hugh and Sophia Auld, and he is enslaved. Sophia Auld has never owned a slave before. She sees a bright child, so she begins to teach him to read.

Then her husband finds out. Douglass later wrote down what he heard Hugh Auld say: that learning would spoil a slave, that a slave who could read would become unmanageable and unhappy, unfit to be kept. Sophia stopped. In time she turned hard against the lessons and would snatch a newspaper out of his hands.

But the boy heard something else inside those angry words. If reading made a person unfit for slavery, then reading was a road out. "From that moment," he wrote, "I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom." The master had told him, without meaning to, exactly what he must do.

So he did it alone, against the whole house. Sent on errands, he carried a book and a piece of bread. Hungry white boys in the streets near the docks were happy to trade a lesson for the bread. He later called it giving them bread in return for "that more valuable bread of knowledge". At about twelve, with fifty cents he had earned, he bought a schoolbook of famous speeches called The Columbian Orator and read it until its words were his own.

Writing came next. In the shipyard he watched carpenters mark the timbers with letters: L for larboard, the left side of the ship, S for starboard, the right. He copied them. He challenged other boys to writing contests on fences and pavements with a lump of chalk. When the house was empty he wrote in the spaces of the old copybooks left by the Aulds' son.

No one gave him permission. Everyone around him said this mind was not meant to be used. He trusted it anyway. In 1838 he escaped to the North, and seven years later he told his story in his own words, and the world read them.

They told him his mind was not his. He spent his life proving it was.
tales.reveals: Douglass trusted his own judgment over the verdict of every adult who held power over him, and turned their warning into his map. His story shows that self-trust is sometimes a quiet, daily act of persistence, one letter at a time.

practice: Before asking anyone's opinion on a decision this week, write down your own view and your reasons first. Then listen, and compare.
Notice one moment when you nod along to something you privately disagree with. Next time, say gently, "I see it differently," and explain why.
Keep a small hunch log: note three intuitions this week and check later which ones held. Learn where your judgment is reliable and where it needs help.
Read a page of Emerson's Self-Reliance and journal: in what part of my life am I living from someone else's script?
principles.shadow: Self-trust can harden into stubbornness or arrogance, a refusal to hear advice, experts or evidence. Trust your mind enough to use it, and humbly enough to change it.

principles.title: Neither raised nor flattened
principles.motto: Let praise and blame pass through you like wind through bamboo.
principles.essence: Good news and bad, praise and insult, will all arrive at your door. Equanimity is not coldness: it is a deep keel that lets you feel the wave without capsizing. You receive what comes, then decide what to keep.
principles.depth: The Buddha named eight worldly winds that blow on every life: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. The quality that stands steady among them is upekkha, usually translated as equanimity, with the sense of looking on evenly. The Tao Te Ching says it in its own way (chapter 58, in my plain rendering): misfortune is what good fortune leans on; good fortune is where misfortune hides. Psychology offers reasons. Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson's research on affective forecasting found that people regularly overestimate how strongly and how long good and bad events will move them, an error they called the impact bias. We adapt faster than we expect, partly thanks to what Gilbert called the psychological immune system. Philip Brickman and colleagues (1978) famously reported that lottery winners were not much happier than others some time later; that study was small, and later research shows adaptation is real but often incomplete, especially after serious illness or losing a job. James Gross's work on emotion regulation (1998) adds that reappraisal, changing how you read an event, eases distress better than pushing the feeling down. Equanimity is not pretending. It is remembering that the story is not over.

tales.title: The Gift Not Taken
tales.who: the Buddha and Akkosaka Bharadvaja, an angry brahmin
tales.where: the Bamboo Grove near Rajagaha, in the ancient kingdom of Magadha (today Bihar, India)
tales.source: Akkosa Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 7.2, in the Pali Canon
tales.tale:
In a grove of bamboo near the city of Rajagaha, the tall stalks creak softly in the wind and the light falls green. Monks sit in the shade with their bowls beside them. Among them is the Buddha, the teacher they follow, resting in the quiet, when a man comes striding down the path, red in the face.

He is a brahmin, a member of the priestly class of ancient India, and the old text calls him Akkosaka Bharadvaja, which means something like Bharadvaja the Abuser. He has heard that a man of his own clan has left home to become a monk under this teacher. To him it is a theft and a shame. He stands before the Buddha and pours out insult after insult, harsh, ugly words, hot as coals from a cooking fire.

The Buddha lets him finish. Then, as the Pali texts tell it, he asks a simple question. "What do you think, brahmin? Do friends and relatives come to visit you as guests?" Yes, sometimes. "And do you offer them food and drink?" Yes, sometimes. "And if they do not accept it, to whom does the food belong?" The brahmin, a little puzzled, answers that it still belongs to him and his household.

"In the same way," the Buddha says, "you have abused me, who does not abuse. You have scolded me, who does not scold. I do not accept it. It is still yours, brahmin. It belongs to you." A person who answers anger with anger, he adds, is like a guest who sits down and eats the meal with the host, sharing the dish of rage. He will not sit down at that table.

The brahmin goes silent. And then, the old story says, this angry man asks to become a monk himself, and in time he too grows calm and clear.

Notice what the Buddha did not do. He did not pretend the words were sweet. He did not strike back. He did not run away, or sulk, or plan revenge. He looked at the gift with steady eyes and left it in the hands of the one who brought it.

An insult is a parcel at your door. You do not have to sign for it.
tales.reveals: Equanimity is not the absence of insult but the freedom not to take it in. The Buddha's calm left room for the angry man to change, which a counterattack never would have done.

tales.title: The Old Man Who Lost His Horse
tales.who: an old man of the frontier (Sai Weng) and his son
tales.where: the northern frontier of China, beside the lands of the Hu horsemen
tales.source: Huainanzi, chapter 18 ("In the World of Men"), compiled at the court of Liu An, King of Huainan
tales.tale:
Out on the northern edge of China, where the farms give way to dry grass and endless wind, an old man lived near the frontier. The Chinese remember him only as Sai Weng, which simply means "the old man of the frontier". Beyond the border roamed the Hu, horse peoples of the steppe. The old man was known as someone who could read the signs of things.

One day his horse broke loose and ran off across the border into the land of the Hu. A horse was wealth, and the neighbors came to comfort him. The old man only said, "How do you know this is not a blessing?" Months passed. Then one morning the horse came trotting home, and behind it came a fine string of Hu horses, strong and fast. Now the neighbors came to congratulate him. The old man said, "How do you know this is not a misfortune?"

His household was rich in good horses, and his son loved to ride. One day the young man fell and broke his hip. He would limp for the rest of his life. Again the neighbors came with long faces. Again the old man said, "How do you know this is not a blessing?"

A year later the Hu came over the border in force. Every able-bodied young man was called to string a bow and fight. Of the men near the frontier, the story says, nine in ten died. The son, because he was lame, stayed home. Father and son both lived, and cared for each other.

The tale comes from the Huainanzi, a great book of Chinese thought gathered at the court of Liu An, King of Huainan, around 139 BC. It is a parable, not a history; no one knows if the old man ever lived. But the Chinese still say, when something goes wrong, that the old man of the frontier lost his horse, and who can tell it was not good fortune?

The old man was not cold. He fed his horses, loved his son, surely grieved and laughed like anyone. He simply refused to close the book after one page.

Fortune is a long road, and on any given day you can see only a short stretch of it.
tales.reveals: The parable shows that we judge events far too quickly, calling them good or bad before their story has finished. Equanimity is the patience to let a day be a day, without crowning it a triumph or a disaster.

practice: When good or bad news comes this week, say the old man's words to yourself, "Who knows if this is good or bad?", and wait a full day before deciding what it means.
If someone criticizes or insults you, picture the untaken gift: keep what is useful, leave the rest with the sender, and reply only once you are calm.
Sit for five minutes each day and simply watch feelings rise and fall, like jeepneys passing on a busy road, without climbing aboard any of them.
Journal: recall a past disaster that turned out better than expected, and a past triumph that brought trouble. What does that teach you about today's news?
principles.shadow: Equanimity can slide into numbness or detachment, a shrug at real harm or a refusal to grieve. Feel fully; the keel is not there to stop the waves, only to keep you upright through them.

principles.title: Want less, and you are rich
principles.motto: Every want you drop is a coin you never have to earn.
principles.essence: Wealth has two sides: what you have and what you want. You can grow rich by gaining more, or, often more easily and more surely, by wanting less. Each need you set down is a chain you no longer have to wear.
principles.depth: Epicurus, in his Letter to Menoeceus, sorted desires into three kinds: natural and necessary (food, shelter, friendship), natural but unnecessary (rich food, fine clothes), and empty (fame, endless wealth), which have no natural limit and so can never be satisfied. Seneca, quoting him in his Letters (21), passed on the advice that to make a man rich you should not add to his money but take away from his desires. Psychology calls the endless chase the hedonic treadmill, a phrase from Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell (1971): as we gain more, our expectations rise and our pleasure drifts back to its old level. Tim Kasser and Richard Ryan (from 1993 onward) found that people who put money, image and status at the center of their goals tend to report lower well-being and more anxiety than those who prize relationships, growth and community. Money does matter, especially when it lifts you out of hardship. Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton (2010) found that day-to-day emotional well-being seemed to level off around a US household income of 75,000 dollars; Matthew Killingsworth (2021) found no such plateau, and a joint 2023 study with Kahneman and Barbara Mellers concluded that the plateau holds mainly for the unhappiest people. Enough is a number you choose, not one the market chooses for you.

tales.title: Out of My Sun
tales.who: Diogenes of Sinope, the Cynic philosopher, and Alexander of Macedon
tales.when: c. 336 BC (the meeting may be legend)
tales.where: the Craneum, a cypress grove and gymnasium outside Corinth, Greece
tales.source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 14; Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, book 6
tales.tale:
Under the cypress trees outside Corinth, an old man lies on the warm ground with his cloak bunched under his head. He owns almost nothing: that cloak, a staff, a bag for scraps of bread. His name is Diogenes, and the Greeks call him the Dog, a Cynic, because he lives in the open like a stray, shameless and free.

He once owned a wooden cup. Then, as the story is told by Diogenes Laertius, an ancient collector of philosophers' lives, he saw a child drinking from a stream with cupped hands. Diogenes threw his cup away. "A child has beaten me in plainness of living," he said.

Now, in about 336 BC, Corinth is full of noise. The Greek cities have gathered there and named a young king, Alexander of Macedon, barely twenty years old, to lead them against the Persian empire. Generals and thinkers crowd around him with praise. Alexander has heard of the Dog, who did not come to bow. So the king goes to find him.

The writer Plutarch, who told this story some four hundred years later, sets the scene: Diogenes lying in the sun, the king and his men coming near, a shadow falling over the old man. Alexander greets him and asks if there is anything he wants. Diogenes raises himself a little on one elbow and says, "Yes. Stand a little out of my sun." Some of the king's men laugh and sneer. But Alexander, as Plutarch tells it, is struck. "If I were not Alexander," he says, "I would be Diogenes."

Historians cannot be sure the meeting happened at all; it may be a tale polished over centuries to make a point. But look at the two men as the point. One will march to India, rule much of the known world, and die at thirty-two in Babylon, still reaching for more. The other wants nothing a king can give, so no king can buy him, frighten him or take anything from him.

The sun on an old man's face cost nothing, and it was the one thing in Corinth that Alexander could not give.

The man who has everything still asks for more. The man who asks for nothing is already full.
tales.reveals: Diogenes was free of Alexander because he wanted nothing Alexander controlled. The story shows that the fewer things you need, the fewer people and circumstances hold power over you.

tales.title: How Many Things I Do Not Need
tales.who: Socrates of Athens; his rival Antiphon
tales.where: the agora, the open market of Athens
tales.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 2.25; Xenophon, Memorabilia 1.6; Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5.91
tales.tale:
The agora of Athens is loud in the morning: fish sellers shouting over silver heaps of sardines, potters setting out red and black jars, sellers of perfume, figs, sandals and cloth dyed purple. Through it all walks a short man with a snub nose, a wide face and bare feet. He wears the same rough cloak summer and winter. His name is Socrates, and he has come not to buy, but to talk.

He stops at the stalls. He looks for a long time at the bright piles of things for sale, the fine shoes, the carved boxes, the scented oils. And then, as Diogenes Laertius tells it, he says to himself, "How many things I can do without!" Cicero, the Roman, tells a similar story of Socrates watching a grand procession of gold and silver and saying, "How many things I do not want." The exact words differ, as old stories do, but the man in them is the same.

He was not poor by accident. He could have charged money for his teaching, as other famous teachers did, and he chose not to. His friend Xenophon wrote down a quarrel with a rival teacher named Antiphon, who mocked him: your food is poor, your cloak is the same in every season, you go without shoes, you take no fees; you are a teacher of misery. Socrates answered that the less a person needs, the freer he is. "You seem to think that happiness consists in luxury," he said, "but I think that to need nothing is divine, and to need as little as possible is closest to the divine."

That freedom gave him something precious: time. He spent his days in the market and the exercise grounds asking questions. What is courage? What is justice? What is a good life? Young men followed him because he could not be bought, and he could not be bought because he wanted so little.

When Athens condemned him to death in 399 BC, he did not have much to leave behind. He had already given away what mattered most, in conversation, for free, to anyone who stopped to listen.

He walked through the busiest market in Greece and came out richer than he went in, carrying nothing.
tales.reveals: Socrates turned the market, a place built to make people want, into a lesson in not wanting. His simplicity was not misery but the price of his freedom: it bought him time, independence and a voice no one could purchase.

practice: Write your own list of enough: the food, shelter, savings and comforts that truly satisfy you. Put a real number on it, and keep it where you will see it.
Take a Socrates walk: go through a mall or market without buying anything, and quietly count the things you can do without.
Try a thirty day pause on one category of wants (gadgets, clothes, online shopping). Write down each urge and see how many survive the month.
Give away or sell five things you have not used in a year, and notice how the empty space feels.
principles.shadow: Wanting little can turn into stinginess, pride in your own plainness, or neglect of the real needs of your family and your future. Enough includes a safety net and room for generosity.

principles.title: Hold all things lightly
principles.motto: Hold life like water in open hands, not a stone in a fist.
principles.essence: Everything you love, and everything you fear, is passing: moods, seasons, fortunes, people, and you. This is not a reason for despair but for tenderness and courage. Hold things with an open hand and you will enjoy them more, and lose them with less damage.
principles.depth: The Buddha named impermanence (anicca) as the first mark of all existence, and taught that suffering grows when we cling to what must change. Heraclitus is remembered for saying you cannot step into the same river twice, and Marcus Aurelius echoed him: time is a river of passing events, and its current is strong (Meditations 4.43). Modern psychology finds that remembering endings can sharpen joy. Laura Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory (developed from the 1990s) shows that when people sense their time is limited, through age, illness or a coming move, they turn toward what matters most, close relationships and present meaning, and often report steadier moods. In a study by Jaime Kurtz (2008), college students asked to think of their graduation as very near did more with their remaining weeks and reported more happiness than students told it was still far off. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, developed by Steven Hayes and colleagues, teaches that struggling to hold on to passing thoughts and feelings tends to make them stickier, while letting them come and go loosens their grip. Economists add the warning of sunk costs: what is already spent and gone should not rule what you choose next. Holding lightly is not loving less. It is loving without strangling.

tales.title: A Notebook in the Plague Years
tales.who: Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor and Stoic
tales.where: army camps on the Danube frontier, and the plague-struck Roman empire
tales.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations (his private notebook, written in Greek, titled To Himself); the physician Galen's descriptions of the plague
tales.tale:
Night in an army camp beside the Danube. Rain on leather tents, the smell of wet horses and woodsmoke. Inside one tent a tired man with a grey beard sits by a lamp and writes, in Greek, not to anyone else, but to himself. He is Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome. And he is reminding himself that all of it will pass.

In about 165 AD, Roman soldiers came home from a war in the east and brought a sickness with them. Today it is called the Antonine Plague, after Marcus's family name. The great physician Galen saw it: fever, dark sores across the skin, and death. It swept the empire for years, through cities and camps alike. Historians still argue about how many died, and many think it was smallpox. Marcus's fellow emperor, Lucius Verus, died suddenly in 169, perhaps of it. Marcus had already buried several of his own children.

And the borders were burning. Germanic tribes crossed the Danube, so Marcus, a bookish man who would rather have stayed with his philosophy, spent most of his last years in cold camps. There he kept the notebook we now call the Meditations. One section ends with a simple note: among the Quadi, by the river Gran. Another: at Carnuntum.

Again and again he writes about change. The universe is change, he tells himself, and life is what our thinking makes it. Think how many doctors have died, he writes, after frowning over so many sickbeds. Hippocrates cured many diseases, and then he too fell sick and died. Time is a river of passing things, and its current is strong: no sooner is a thing seen than it is swept away, and another comes in its place.

Once he wrote of plague directly. A sickness of the air is bad, he said, but a sickness of the mind is worse, because it attacks what makes us human. The plague might take his body. He would not let fear and cruelty take his character.

He died in 180 AD, still on campaign, perhaps of the same plague. He never meant the notebook for us. It survived anyway, and has kept company with the grieving and the frightened ever since.

He held an empire in his hands, and each night he wrote himself a lesson in opening them.
tales.reveals: Surrounded by death and war, Marcus used the truth of impermanence not to despair but to steady himself and do his duty. Remembering that everything passes made him gentler with others and less afraid for himself.

tales.title: The Moon the Thief Left Behind
tales.who: Ryokan, a Zen monk and poet, and a thief
tales.when: early 19th century (the anecdote is likely legend; the poem is his)
tales.where: Gogo-an, a hut on Mount Kugami, Echigo province (today Niigata), Japan
tales.source: Ryokan's haiku about the thief and the moon; the anecdote is told in Japanese tradition and in Zen story collections
tales.tale:
Snow on the mountain, and a hut so small that the wind slips in through its walls. Inside sits a thin old monk in a patched robe. His name is Ryokan. He lived from 1758 to 1831 in Echigo, a snowy province on the Sea of Japan coast, and for many years he made his home in a little hermitage called Gogo-an on Mount Kugami. He begged for his rice in the villages, played ball and hide and seek with the children, wrote poems, and owned almost nothing.

One night, the story says, a thief crept into the hut. He searched every corner. There was a bowl, a cushion, a few books, nothing worth carrying away. Ryokan woke and saw the man, and saw his disappointment. He did not shout. You came all this way, he said, or so the tale goes, and you should not leave with empty hands. He took off his own robe and held it out. The bewildered thief grabbed it and ran into the dark.

Ryokan sat by his window, bare in the cold, looking at the moon over the mountain. "Poor fellow," he said. "I wish I could have given him this beautiful moon."

That is the story as it has been handed down. Whether the robe and the words really happened, no one can say; the tale may have grown up around a poem. But the poem is truly Ryokan's, one of his short haiku, and in plain English it says: the thief left it behind, the moon in my window.

Think of that night. The thief took what could be carried. The hut was a little emptier, and colder. Yet the thing that filled the window, the silver light on the snow, was never Ryokan's to lose and never anyone's to take. He had spent his life practising letting go, so when something was taken, there was little to tear.

Everything you own will leave you one day: by theft, by wear, by time, or by your own going. You cannot stop that. You can choose what you lean your heart on.

The robe was gone by morning. The moon comes back every month.
tales.reveals: Ryokan's lightness about his few possessions let him meet a theft with pity instead of rage. The tale shows that holding things loosely does not make life poorer; it turns your attention to what can never be taken.

practice: Each evening, name one thing from the day you enjoyed and tell yourself, "This will not come again in just this way." Let the thought sharpen your gratitude, not your sadness.
When a hard mood comes, name it ("this is worry") and remind yourself that moods are weather, like a passing rain squall, not the whole climate of your life.
Hold one possession lightly on purpose this week: lend a book, share a tool, or give away something you would secretly like to keep.
Write a few lines to yourself tonight, as Marcus did, about something you are clinging to, and what loosening your grip would look like.
principles.shadow: Holding lightly can become not holding at all: avoiding commitment, love or responsibility because everything passes anyway. Grip gently, but do grip; care fully for what is here while it is here.

principles.title: Learn to make and mend
principles.motto: What your hands can mend, the world cannot take from you.
principles.essence: Every thing you can make, fix or patch is a small freedom: one less need you must buy, one less stranger you must wait for. Learn the simple crafts of keeping a life in working order, and let the mended places carry their story with pride.
principles.depth: Albert Bandura (1977) found that the surest source of self-efficacy, the belief that you can handle what comes, is mastery experience: doing a hard thing yourself and seeing it work. A fixed faucet teaches your nervous system something no pep talk can. Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely (2012) named the "IKEA effect": people value things they have built themselves far above identical things made by others. Labour turns objects into something close to companions, and we look after companions. Thoreau put the economics plainly in Walden: "the cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it, immediately or in the long run." Each repair you can do yourself is life you do not have to sell. Matthew Crawford, in Shop Class as Soulcraft (2009), argued that manual work keeps us honest, because a bolt either holds or it does not, and no amount of talk will change that. The Japanese sense of wabi-sabi, the beauty of things worn, humble and incomplete, adds a gentler lesson: wear and repair are not shame but history. To mend something is to say that things, and people, are worth keeping.

tales.title: Twenty-eight dollars and twelve and a half cents
tales.who: Henry David Thoreau
tales.where: Walden Pond, Concord, Massachusetts
tales.source: Thoreau, Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854), chapter "Economy"
tales.tale:
At the end of March, when the ice on Walden Pond was still dark and full of holes, a young man walked into the woods with a borrowed axe on his shoulder. He was twenty-seven. His name was Henry David Thoreau, and people in Concord thought him clever, odd, and not much use.

He chose a hillside of tall white pines above the water and began to cut. He shaped the timbers square, posts and rafters, and cut the joints himself. At noon he sat among the green branches he had trimmed and ate his bread and butter. His hands were thick with pine pitch, and so, he wrote, his bread took on the fragrance of the woods.

For boards he bought the shanty of James Collins, an Irishman who worked on the railroad, for four dollars and twenty-five cents. Early one morning he took it apart, pulled the nails, and carried the boards to his hillside, laying them on the grass to bleach and straighten in the sun. In May a few friends came to help raise the frame. He asked them, he said, less from need than to enjoy a good chance for neighbourliness.

By the Fourth of July, 1845, he was living in it. The house was ten feet wide and fifteen long, with an attic, a closet, a large window on each side and a door at one end. He kept every cost in his notebook, down to the half cent, and printed the list in his book: nails, three dollars and ninety cents; hinges and screws, fourteen cents; chalk, one cent; hair to mix into the plaster, thirty-one cents, "more than I needed." The total was twenty-eight dollars and twelve and a half cents. A student at Harvard, he pointed out, paid about thirty dollars a year just to rent a room hardly bigger than his.

The land was not his. It belonged to his friend Ralph Waldo Emerson, and Thoreau never hid that. But the walls were his in a deeper way. He knew every board, because his own hands had set it there. He had learned, by doing, how little a shelter truly needs, and how much of a life is spent paying for what others build.

When the work was done, he gave the axe back to its owner. He returned it, he wrote, sharper than he received it.
tales.reveals: Making his own house showed Thoreau exactly what a home costs, in money and in life, and freed him from paying more than he had to. Even his independence was built with borrowed tools and friendly hands, and he honoured that by giving back more than he took.

tales.title: The bowl with rivers of gold
tales.who: Ashikaga Yoshimasa, eighth shogun of Japan, and the craftsmen of the tea tradition
tales.where: Kyoto, Japan, and Ming China
tales.source: Japanese tea lore; the stapled bowl Bakohan, whose story Ito Togai wrote down in 1727 (Tokyo National Museum)
tales.tale:
Picture a tea bowl the colour of a spring sky seen through water. It is Chinese celadon, a pale green-blue glaze, thick and cool in the hand, and it belongs to the most powerful man in Japan. One day a crack runs through it, like lightning caught in glass.

The man was Ashikaga Yoshimasa, the eighth shogun, who ruled from Kyoto in the 1400s. He was a weak ruler in many ways; war burned through his city while he built gardens and watched the moon. But he loved beautiful things, and he loved that bowl.

As the story is told, he sent it back across the sea to China and asked for another just like it. No potter there could match it. So the bowl came home mended in the plain way of the time: small holes drilled on either side of the crack, and metal staples clamped across it like stitches on a wound. It held tea again. Some found it ugly. Others came to treasure it, saying the staples looked like a locust resting on the glaze.

From here the legend runs further. Japanese craftsmen, it says, looked at those staples and asked whether a repair could be as lovely as the thing it repaired. They turned to urushi, a lacquer made from the sap of a tree, which dries as hard as stone. They filled the cracks with it and dusted the wet lacquer with powdered gold. The break did not hide. It shone. And so, the tale goes, kintsugi was born, which means "golden joinery."

Here is the honest part. The stapled bowl is real. It is called Bakohan, it rests today in the Tokyo National Museum, and a scholar named Ito Togai wrote its story down in 1727, more than two hundred years after Yoshimasa. But no record proves that this bowl gave birth to gold repair. Kintsugi seems to have grown slowly among tea masters of the 1500s and 1600s, who prized rough, humble, imperfect things.

What those tea masters understood is the part worth keeping. A cracked bowl, carefully mended, has lived a life. Its golden lines are a map of where it broke, and of the patient hands that would not throw it away.

The bowl is not beautiful in spite of the break. It is beautiful because someone stayed.
tales.reveals: Mending is not only thrift; it is a way of seeing, in which repair adds value instead of hiding loss. The legend also shows how a humble fix, done with care, can become an art that outlives the person who first needed it.

practice: Learn one repair this week that you would normally pay for or throw away: sew on a button, patch a shirt, reglue a tsinelas strap, or replace a leaking faucet washer. Watch one good tutorial, then do it with your own hands.
Make a small mending box with needle and thread, strong glue, electrical tape, a screwdriver set and a few spare screws, and keep it where you can reach it without searching.
Before you replace anything broken, wait three days and ask: can this be mended, by me or by a repair shop in the neighbourhood? Write down what you saved.
Make one simple thing from scratch, such as a shelf, a cloth bag, a basket or a meal from raw ingredients, and journal how it feels to use something you made.
principles.shadow: Make-and-mend turns sour when it becomes pride that refuses all help, or stubbornness that spends a week on a job a skilled neighbour could do in an hour. Mend what you can, pay or trade for what you cannot, and honour the craftspeople around you.

principles.title: Know where your food comes from
principles.motto: A seed in your hand is a promise you can keep.
principles.essence: Food is the most basic dependence of all, and most of us have forgotten where ours begins. Learn how food grows, grow a little of your own, and you will eat with more gratitude, more health and less fear.
principles.depth: Knowing your food works on three levels. First, the body: in a randomised trial in Denver, Jill Litt and colleagues (2023, The Lancet Planetary Health) found that adults assigned to community gardening ate more fibre and reported less stress and anxiety than a waiting-list group. A meta-analysis by Masashi Soga, Kevin Gaston and Yuichi Yamaura (2017) linked gardening to lower depression and anxiety and higher life satisfaction, though many of its studies were small. Second, the mind: psychologists describe "psychological ownership", the bond that forms when you invest effort in something, which is why a tomato you raised tastes of more than tomato. Third, resilience: a home with even a few pots of kangkong, malunggay and camote has a small buffer when prices jump or a typhoon cuts the roads. Philosophy agrees. Epicurus wrote to Menoeceus that bread and water give the highest pleasure to someone truly hungry, and that a taste for simple food frees us from fear of losing luxuries. Thoreau grew beans at Walden because he was "determined to know beans." The farmer and essayist Wendell Berry later argued that every meal is part of farming, whether we see the farm or not. To know your food is to stop being only a customer of your own life.

tales.title: The man who did nothing to the rice
tales.who: Masanobu Fukuoka
tales.where: Iyo, Ehime Prefecture, on the island of Shikoku, Japan
tales.source: Fukuoka's own account in The One-Straw Revolution (Japanese 1975, English 1978) and later interviews
tales.tale:
Before dawn one spring morning in 1937, a young scientist sat beneath a tree on a hill above the harbour at Yokohama. He had wandered all night, unable to sleep, still weak from pneumonia and tangled in questions about life and death. Then a night heron cried out over the water, and something in him broke open. Everything he thought he knew, he felt, was nothing beside the living world itself.

His name was Masanobu Fukuoka, and he was a plant inspector at the customs office. Soon after, he left his job and went home to his father's farm in Iyo, on the island of Shikoku, where mandarin orange trees climbed the hillsides above the sea.

His first experiment failed. Wanting to let nature lead, he stopped pruning part of his father's orchard. The trees, long shaped by human hands, grew tangled, insects moved in, and many died. He learned a lesson he never forgot: you cannot simply walk away from something you have already changed. You must learn, slowly, how to step back.

After the war he spent more than thirty years on that learning. He stopped ploughing. He used no chemical fertiliser and no poison sprays. In autumn he scattered rice seed and white clover among the ripening barley, and after the harvest he threw the barley straw back over the fields, loose and uncut, to feed the soil. Later he rolled seeds into little balls of clay so birds would leave them alone until the rain came. Neighbours shook their heads. Then they came to look, because his fields, by his own account, gave rice harvests close to the best in the district, with far less labour.

He wrote it all down in a small book, The One-Straw Revolution, published in Japan in 1975, and soon people around the world were reading it. Not everyone could repeat his results; soil, climate and patience differ from place to place. But his deeper point travelled well.

A farmer who watches closely, season after season, grows something besides grain. He grows attention. He comes to know the rain by its smell and the soil by the way it crumbles in his palm.

Fukuoka died in 2008, aged ninety-five, having spent his long life listening to one hillside. The hillside, in its quiet way, had answered.
tales.reveals: Knowing where food comes from can go far deeper than reading a label: it can become a lifetime of attention to soil, seasons and living things. Fukuoka's failures mattered as much as his successes, because they taught him to work with nature instead of either forcing it or abandoning it.

tales.title: Cabbages in the castle moat
tales.who: Ordinary households in Britain and the United States; Eleanor Roosevelt
tales.where: Britain and the United States
tales.source: Britain's "Dig for Victory" campaign (Ministry of Agriculture); US Department of Agriculture estimates; newspapers of 1943
tales.tale:
Imagine London in 1940: sandbags piled at the doors, black cloth over every window at night, and in the dry moat of the Tower of London, where soldiers once marched, neat green rows of cabbages.

When the Second World War began in 1939, Britain brought much of its food by ship, and enemy submarines were sinking those ships. The government did more than ration sugar, butter and meat. It handed people a spade. Under the slogan "Dig for Victory," posters showed a boot pushing a garden fork into dark earth. Lawns became potato beds. Railway banks, school fields and corners of Hyde Park were dug up. The number of allotments, small rented garden plots, rose from about eight hundred thousand to nearly one and a half million.

Across the ocean, the United States did the same after it joined the war in 1941. Families called them Victory Gardens. In 1943 Eleanor Roosevelt, the president's wife, had one planted on the White House lawn, though the Secretary of Agriculture, it is reported, worried it would hurt farmers and food sellers. Children grew beans in school plots. Office workers kept tomatoes on rooftops. Government figures from the time estimated that some twenty million gardens grew around forty percent of the fresh vegetables Americans ate. The number is hard to check, but the scale was real.

Something grew in those gardens besides food. Neighbours who had never spoken traded seeds over fences. Old people who remembered farm life taught young clerks how far apart to sow carrots. Fear, which had nowhere to go, went into the soil, and came back up green.

Then the war ended. Rationing eased, the shops filled again, and most of the gardens went back to grass. Within a few years many people forgot that they had once helped to feed their countries from their own back yards.

But the lesson waits in the ground for anyone who needs it. A nation is fed by its farmers. In a hard season it can also be fed, in part, by its people, one row of beans at a time.
tales.reveals: When supply lines fail, the knowledge of how to grow food becomes a form of security that no one can ration. The gardens also show that self-reliance in food is strongest when it is shared, passed between neighbours and generations.

practice: Grow one edible plant this week, even on a windowsill or balcony: kangkong in a basin of water, malunggay from a cutting, camote tops in a pot, or pechay from seed.
Go to the palengke early one morning and ask a vendor where their vegetables or fish came from and how far they travelled. Trace three items in your kitchen back to a province.
Cook one dish entirely from raw ingredients whose source you know, such as ginisang monggo or a simple sinigang, then teach it to someone younger.
Journal: if the shops closed for two weeks after a typhoon, what would you eat, and which one skill or plant would make that easier?
principles.shadow: Growing your own can turn into a purity contest, or a proud refusal to buy from the farmers whose work feeds you. Grow a little, learn a lot, and stay grateful to the many hands that grow the rest.

principles.title: The body is the first home
principles.motto: Carry the calf each day, and one day you carry the bull.
principles.essence: Your body is the one home you will never move out of, and everything else you do rests on its strength. Tend it daily with movement, rest, plain food and gradual challenge, and it will carry you further than you think.
principles.depth: The body adapts to what you ask of it, a little at a time. Hans Selye's research on stress, from the 1930s on, described how living things respond to a strain and then recover; trainers call the useful version of this progressive overload, and Nassim Nicholas Taleb (2012) gave the wider idea a name: antifragility. The key word is manageable. Too little load and nothing changes; too much and you break. The rewards reach far beyond muscle. In the PURE study, Darryl Leong and colleagues (2015, The Lancet) followed nearly 140,000 adults in 17 countries and found that weaker grip strength predicted earlier death and heart disease. James Blumenthal and colleagues (1999) found that sixteen weeks of aerobic exercise eased major depression in older adults about as well as the drug sertraline, and a large 2024 review by Michael Noetel and colleagues in The BMJ found that walking, jogging, yoga and strength training all reduced depression, though the quality of the studies varied. The Stoics knew this. Musonius Rufus taught that a philosopher must train the body along with the soul, through cold, heat, hunger and hard work, because a body that can endure gives the mind room to stay calm. Strength is not vanity. It is freedom of movement for your whole life.

tales.title: The calf that became a bull
tales.who: Milo of Croton, wrestler
tales.where: Croton, a Greek city in southern Italy, and Olympia
tales.source: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria (c. AD 95); Athenaeus, The Deipnosophists; Pausanias, Description of Greece; Diodorus of Sicily
tales.tale:
On a hillside above the sea in southern Italy, a young man bends, wraps his arms around a newborn calf, and lifts it onto his shoulders. The calf kicks once, then goes still. He walks a slow circle and sets it down. Tomorrow he will lift it again.

The young man was Milo, of the Greek city of Croton, and he became the most famous wrestler of the ancient world. He won at the Olympic Games six times, first as a boy and then as a man, across some twenty-four years in the late 500s BC. A statue of him stood at Olympia, and the story goes that he carried it into the sacred grove himself.

The tale of the calf comes from the Roman teacher Quintilian, writing about six hundred years later. Milo, he says, grew used to carrying a calf, and so was able to carry it when it was a bull. It is almost certainly a legend. A calf gains hundreds of kilos in a few years, far faster than any human can add strength. But the legend has lasted because it holds a truth every trainer knows: the load must grow a little at a time, never all at once, and you must show up every day.

Other old writers added colour. Athenaeus says that at Olympia Milo carried a four-year-old bull around the stadium on his shoulders, then ate the whole of it in a single day. Diodorus says he led Croton's army into battle wearing his Olympic crowns and a lion skin, like the hero Heracles. These are wilder tales, and no one can prove them.

The old story of his death is a warning. As an old man, walking alone in a forest, Milo found a tree trunk that woodcutters had begun to split, held open with wedges. He pushed his hands into the crack to tear it apart. The wedges fell out, the wood snapped shut on his fingers, and he was trapped there, the story says, until wolves found him.

Strength built slowly served him all his life. Strength trusted blindly, long past its season, was his undoing.

Carry the calf each day. And know, too, when it is time to set the bull down.
tales.reveals: The body grows strong through small, steady increases, not heroic bursts. Milo's legendary death adds the other half of the lesson: real strength includes knowing your limits as the years change you.

tales.title: The boy they called a stick
tales.who: Fauja Singh, marathon runner, and his coach Harmander Singh
tales.where: Beas Pind, Punjab, India; Ilford, London; Toronto, Canada
tales.source: Newspaper reports (BBC, The Guardian, Toronto Star); Khushwant Singh's biography Turbaned Tornado (2011)
tales.tale:
As a small boy in a village in Punjab, Fauja Singh could barely walk. His legs were thin and weak, and other children called him danda, which means a stick. He did not walk properly, it is said, until he was about five.

He grew up to be a farmer in the flat fields of Beas Pind, near the city of Jalandhar, and as a young man he loved to run. Then for decades he stopped. He married, raised children, worked the land, and grew old in the ordinary way.

Grief changed his road. His wife died, and in 1994 his son Kuldip was killed in an accident before his eyes. Fauja, past eighty, was lost. He moved to Ilford, in East London, to live with another son. There, to fill the empty hours and quiet his sorrow, he began to walk, and then to run again.

A coach named Harmander Singh trained him for the London Marathon, and in 2000, at the age of eighty-nine by his passport, Fauja ran it in about six hours and fifty-four minutes. He kept going. In Toronto in 2003, at ninety-two, he finished in five hours and forty minutes. And on a cold October morning in 2011, again in Toronto, in a bright turban with his white beard down his chest, he crossed the finish line of a full marathon at the age of one hundred. It had taken him more than eight hours. Long after most runners had gone home, the crowd at the line cheered him in as if he had won.

Guinness World Records did not list the feat, because villages in India did not issue birth certificates in 1911, and his only proof of age was his passport. Some doubt the exact number. No one doubts the miles.

His habits were plain: early to bed, a long walk every day, simple vegetarian food such as dal and roti, and ginger tea. He ran his last race, ten kilometres in Hong Kong, in 2013, then kept walking for many years. He died in July 2025, struck by a vehicle while crossing a road near his home village. By his passport, he was one hundred and fourteen.

The boy they called a stick had walked, and then run, his way around the world.
tales.reveals: It is never too late to begin caring for the body, and movement can carry a person through grief as well as across a finish line. Fauja Singh's plain habits show that a strong body is built from ordinary daily choices, not special secrets.

practice: Choose one daily "calf": ten slow squats, a short plank, or carrying a full water container up the stairs. Add one repetition or a few seconds every few days, never more.
Walk for thirty minutes each day this week, early in the morning or after sunset when the heat is gentler, with your phone in your pocket.
Test yourself once and write it down: how long you can hang from a bar, how many push-ups you can do (even against a wall), how long you can stand on one leg. Test again in a month.
Guard your sleep for seven nights: the same bedtime, screens off thirty minutes before, and a note each morning on your mood and patience.
principles.shadow: Care for the body can harden into vanity, punishing routines or contempt for those who are weaker, ill or old. Train so that your body can serve your life, rest when it asks, and see a doctor when you need one.

principles.title: Teach yourself anything
principles.motto: Every master was first a beginner who would not stop asking.
principles.essence: You need no one's permission to learn. With a good model, honest feedback and steady practice, you can teach yourself almost any skill, and the habit of self-teaching is the skill that unlocks all the others.
principles.depth: Self-teaching works best when it follows how memory is actually built. Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke (2006) showed that students who tested themselves on a passage remembered far more a week later than students who simply reread it: the act of recalling is what makes learning stick. Norman Slamecka and Peter Graf (1978) found a "generation effect": words you produce yourself are remembered better than words you only read. K. Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Römer (1993) argued that expert skill grows from deliberate practice, focused effort at the edge of your ability with quick feedback. That claim is debated: a 2014 meta-analysis by Brooke Macnamara, David Hambrick and Frederick Oswald found that practice explained only part of the differences between people, so talent, timing and good teachers matter too. Still, the method helps anyone improve on their own starting point. Philosophy adds both caution and courage. Socrates taught that wisdom begins with knowing what you do not know. Emerson wrote in "Self-Reliance" that "there is a time in every man's education when he arrives at the conviction that envy is ignorance; that imitation is suicide." Yet Emerson learned from every book he loved. Imitate in order to learn, then leave the model behind and find your own voice.

tales.title: The boy who rebuilt The Spectator
tales.who: Benjamin Franklin, apprentice printer, and his father Josiah
tales.where: Boston, Massachusetts
tales.source: Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography (begun 1771, published after his death)
tales.tale:
In a Boston printing shop, after the presses have gone quiet, a boy of about sixteen sits with a worn book and a stack of paper. His fingers are black with ink. He is not reading for pleasure. He is taking the book apart.

The boy was Benjamin Franklin, apprentice to his older brother James, a printer. He had left school at ten. He loved to argue, and he and a friend named John Collins had been trading letters, each trying to win a debate. Their father, Josiah Franklin, found the letters and read them. He did not take sides. Instead he told Benjamin that his writing fell short in elegance, in method and in clearness. The boy saw that his father was right.

Around that time he came across an odd volume of The Spectator, the London paper of short essays by Joseph Addison and Richard Steele. "It was the third," Franklin wrote many years later. "I had never before seen any of them. I bought it, read it over and over, and was much delighted with it."

Then he invented a way to learn from it. He took an essay and wrote short hints of the meaning of each sentence. He set the hints aside for a few days. Then, without looking at the book, he tried to write the essay again in full, in his own words. Afterwards he laid his version beside the original and hunted for every fault. When he found he lacked words, he turned the essays into verse, which forces you to search for words that fit the rhythm, and later turned the verse back into prose. When he found his thinking out of order, he shuffled his hints and tried to put them back in the best order.

He worked at night after the shop closed, in the early morning before it opened, and on Sundays, when he managed to stay alone in the printing house instead of going to church. Sometimes, he admitted with quiet pleasure, he thought he had improved on the original in some small point.

No teacher marked his pages. The book was his teacher, and his own honest eye was the examiner.

That boy grew into one of the finest writers of his century. He began with a borrowed voice, and from it, patiently, he built his own.
tales.reveals: Franklin's method holds the whole craft of self-teaching: a good model, an attempt from memory, honest comparison and correction. It also began with a hard truth from his father, received without sulking, which shows that teaching yourself still means listening to others.

tales.title: Five thousand doors
tales.who: Srinivasa Ramanujan, and the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy
tales.where: Kumbakonam and Madras (now Chennai), India; Cambridge, England
tales.source: G. H. Hardy's writings on Ramanujan (1921, 1940); Ramanujan's notebooks and letters; later biographies
tales.tale:
On the narrow front porch of a small house in Kumbakonam, in the south of India, a teenage boy sits with a slate on his knees. He writes, rubs the chalk away with his elbow, and writes again. Paper costs money, and his family has little. By the end of the day, as the story is told, his elbow is rough and dark.

The boy was Srinivasa Ramanujan. At about fifteen he borrowed a book that changed his life: A Synopsis of Elementary Results in Pure and Applied Mathematics, by George Shoobridge Carr, a London tutor who had made it to help students cram for exams. It was not a friendly book. It listed thousands of formulas and theorems, five or six thousand by different counts, one after another, with almost no explanation and very few proofs.

For most readers it would have been a wall. For Ramanujan it was a row of doors. Each bare result was a question: why is this true? He set out to prove them himself, with no teacher at all. Along the way he began to find results that were in no book, things no one had ever seen. He filled notebook after notebook.

His self-teaching had a price. He became so absorbed in mathematics that he neglected every other subject. He won a scholarship to the college in Kumbakonam and lost it after failing his exams. He tried again at a college in Madras and failed again. For years he was poor, sometimes hungry, living on small help from friends and patrons, until he found work as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust.

In January 1913 he wrote to G. H. Hardy, a leading mathematician at Cambridge, sending pages of formulas. At first Hardy wondered if it was the work of a crank. Then he looked closer. Some of the results, he later wrote, had to be true, because no one could have had the imagination to invent them. In 1914 he brought Ramanujan to England.

At Cambridge, Hardy had to teach him what Carr's book had left out: the slow craft of careful proof. Ramanujan learned it, and in 1918 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. Worn by illness, cold and poor food, he went home and died in 1920, aged thirty-two.

He taught himself to reach the very edge of mathematics. It took a friend to help him step across.
tales.reveals: A single bare book was enough for Ramanujan to teach himself, because he turned every statement into a question and refused to stop until he understood it. His story is also honest about the cost and the limits of learning alone: his genius flowered fully only when a teacher filled the gaps he could not see.

practice: Pick one skill you have always wanted, such as basic accounting, a new language, swimming or simple electrical work, and spend twenty focused minutes on it every day this week.
Try Franklin's method on anything you want to master: study a good example, put it away, rebuild it from memory, then compare and correct.
After reading or watching a lesson, close it and write down or say aloud everything you remember before you look again. Recall is where the learning happens.
Find one person a step or two ahead of you in the skill and ask them to look at your work once. Journal: what did they see that you could not?
principles.shadow: Self-teaching can become arrogance that scorns teachers, or isolation that keeps you repeating the same mistakes for years. Teach yourself boldly, but seek out feedback, mentors and the knowledge others have already won.

principles.title: Prepare in the fat years
principles.motto: Fill the granary while the sun shines; winter makes no promises.
principles.essence: Good times do not last forever, and neither do bad ones. Use the seasons of plenty to store up what the lean seasons will ask of you, savings, supplies, skills and friendships, so that hardship finds you steady instead of surprised.
principles.depth: We are built to favour today. Economists call it present bias: David Laibson (1997) modelled how people discount the future steeply, choosing a small reward now over a larger one later, and then regretting it. Walter Mischel's marshmallow studies, begun around 1970, seemed to show that children who could wait did better in life, but a larger replication by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan (2018) found the link much weaker once family background was taken into account. The lesson is not that some people are born patient, but that circumstances and systems shape our ability to wait. So build systems: an automatic saving, a stocked shelf, a plan made in calm weather. Amartya Sen, in Poverty and Famines (1981), showed that famines such as Bengal's in 1943 often struck not because food ran out but because poor people lost the means to obtain it. Readiness, then, is about reserves you can reach when you need them: cash, skills, and people who will share. The Stoics practised premeditatio malorum, thinking ahead about misfortune, and Seneca urged in his letters that we rehearse hardship while life is easy, so that it does not catch us unprepared. Preparation is not fear. It is the calm that fear cannot borrow.

tales.title: Seven fat cows, seven lean
tales.who: Joseph, son of Jacob, and the Pharaoh of Egypt
tales.when: ancient (scripture; no date can be fixed)
tales.where: Egypt
tales.source: Genesis 41 and 47 (King James Version quoted)
tales.tale:
A king wakes in the dark, his heart pounding. He has dreamed that he stood by the river Nile, and out of the water came seven cows, sleek and fat, grazing in the reeds. Then seven more came up behind them, bony and ugly and starved. And the thin cows ate the fat ones, and were no fatter for it.

He slept again and dreamed of seven full, golden ears of grain on a single stalk, and seven thin ears, scorched by the east wind, that swallowed them up. No one in his court could tell him what it meant.

Then his chief butler remembered a young Hebrew in prison, a slave named Joseph, sold long ago by his own brothers, who had once explained the butler's dream truly. Joseph was shaved, dressed and brought before Pharaoh. The two dreams, he said, are one. Seven years of great plenty are coming to Egypt, and after them seven years of famine so heavy that the plenty will be forgotten.

He did not stop at the warning. He offered a plan. Let a wise man be set over the land, he said, to gather a fifth part of the harvest in the good years and store it in the cities, so "that the land perish not through the famine." Pharaoh chose Joseph himself. He was thirty years old.

For seven years Joseph filled the storehouses. He "gathered corn as the sand of the sea, very much, until he left numbering; for it was without number." When the lean years came and the fields cracked, Egypt had bread, and "all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn." Among them, at last, came his own hungry brothers.

The story has a darker chapter, often skipped. In Genesis 47, as the famine dragged on, Joseph traded the grain for the people's money, then their cattle, then their land, until the Egyptians said they would be Pharaoh's servants. A store held in one hand can become power over many.

This is scripture, not a record historians can confirm; no Egyptian text describes it. But its wisdom is plain enough for any household. The time to prepare for the lean years is while the cows are fat.
tales.reveals: Joseph's gift was not only seeing the famine coming but turning a warning into a patient, practical plan. The darker chapter is a reminder that reserves should make people more secure, not more dependent on whoever holds the keys.

tales.title: The song of summer and the long cold
tales.who: Aesop's ant and grasshopper (in the Greek, a cicada)
tales.when: legend (Aesop is said to have lived in the 6th century BC)
tales.where: ancient Greece
tales.source: Aesop's Fables (Perry Index 373); Herodotus, Histories, book 2; La Fontaine, Fables (1668); Proverbs 6:6 (King James Version)
tales.tale:
All summer long, in the dry grass at the edge of a wheat field, the grasshopper sang. The sun was hot, the stalks were heavy, and life seemed as if it would always be golden. Below him a line of ants moved back and forth, back and forth, each one carrying a single grain to the nest under the ground.

"Why work so hard?" the grasshopper called down. "Come and sing. There is food everywhere."

The ants did not stop. Winter is coming, they said, and they kept on carrying.

Then the rains came, and the frost, and the field lay bare and grey. The grasshopper, thin and shivering, came to the ants' door and begged for a little grain. "What were you doing all summer?" the ants asked. "I was singing," he said. "Then," they answered, "you may dance all winter." And they shut the door.

That is the fable as it has been told for some two and a half thousand years. It is credited to Aesop, a Greek storyteller who, according to the historian Herodotus, was once a slave on the island of Samos; whether he made any of the fables we have, no one knows. In the old Greek versions the singer is a cicada, the insect whose buzzing fills hot afternoons, and the French poet Jean de La Fontaine kept the cicada in 1668; English tellers often turned it into a grasshopper. Long before, the Book of Proverbs had said something similar: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise."

The lesson is clear. The ant prepares in the season of plenty, and the grasshopper does not. But readers have long been troubled by the ending. The ants are right, and they are also cold. They have grain to spare, and they offer only a joke.

A wiser reading takes both creatures seriously. Be the ant in summer: store, save, prepare. But do not become the ant at the door. The grasshopper's song is part of what makes summer worth saving for, and a full storehouse is best used, in part, to open the door.
tales.reveals: The fable teaches that the season of plenty is the time to prepare, because the season of want will not wait. Read wisely, it also warns that preparation without kindness becomes its own kind of poverty.

practice: Build a typhoon kit this week: water for three days (about four litres per person per day), canned food, a flashlight, a charged power bank, medicines, copies of IDs in a sealed plastic pouch, and some cash in small bills.
Set up one automatic transfer on payday, however small, into a separate emergency fund, and give it a target: first one month of expenses, then three, then six.
Write a "lean years" list: if your income stopped tomorrow, which costs could you cut, which skills could earn, and whom could you call? Strengthen one item on it this month.
Journal: who in my family or barangay would struggle most in a disaster, and how could my preparations include them?
principles.shadow: Readiness can curdle into hoarding, constant worry, or the ant's shut door: a life spent guarding against a future that is never allowed to arrive. Prepare enough to stand steady, then live freely today and share from what you have stored.

principles.title: Live below your means
principles.motto: Spend less than you earn, and the gap becomes your freedom.
principles.essence: Live a little below what you earn, on purpose, and let the gap grow quiet and wide. The space between your income and your spending is not a sacrifice: it is the room where your freedom, your calm and your generosity live.
principles.depth: Most of what we spend on rises to meet our income, then stops feeling special. Psychologists call this hedonic adaptation: Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell named the 'hedonic treadmill' in 1971, and a 1978 study of lottery winners by Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman found them not much happier than others some time later (a small study, often over-told, though the wider pattern of adaptation has held up). Money still matters: Matthew Killingsworth, Daniel Kahneman and Barbara Mellers (2023) found that well-being keeps rising with income for most people. But every step up in lifestyle also raises the floor you must defend each month. A gap between income and spending works differently. It buys slack, what Sendhil Mullainathan and Eldar Shafir call the spare room that lets the mind think beyond the next bill. Seneca, one of the richest men in Rome, saw the danger clearly: not owning things, but needing them. Epicurus taught that self-sufficiency is a great good, not so that we always live on little, but so that if we must, we are not afraid. Living below your means is that teaching turned into a monthly habit.

tales.title: The Rehearsal of Poverty
tales.who: Seneca, Roman philosopher and statesman, writing to his friend Lucilius
tales.where: Rome, during the December festival of Saturnalia
tales.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 18 (English quotation from Richard Gummere's translation, 1917)
tales.tale:
It is December in Rome, and the whole city is sweating with feast. The Saturnalia has come, the festival when slaves dine beside their masters, when the streets fill with dice and shouting, when everyone seems to have agreed, for a few days, to eat too much.

In the middle of this noise an old man sits down to write a letter. His name is Seneca. He is a philosopher, and he is also one of the richest men in the empire, an adviser who has stood close to the emperor Nero and grown wealthy beside him. He writes to his younger friend Lucilius, an official in Sicily, and what he writes is strange advice for a rich man to give.

Set aside a few days, he says. Eat the plainest food, and not much of it. Wear the roughest cloak you own. Sleep on a hard bed. And while you do it, ask yourself one question. In Richard Gummere's old English translation it reads: 'Is this the condition that I feared?'

Seneca is careful. He does not mean a show. He does not mean the fashionable game some rich Romans played, eating from clay dishes in a pretty room built to look poor. He means real hard bread, a real hard bed, real days. The soldier, he says, trains in time of peace, marching and digging when no enemy is near, so that the battle will not find him soft. Let poverty find you already trained.
